abstract: Individuals of the same chronological age present different trajectories of age-related physiological and mental decline, suggesting a distinction between chronological age and the aging process. Biological age, estimated from molecular and physiological biomarkers, has been proposed to represent human aging better than chronological age. Prior research has mainly focused on identifying biomarkers of aging from a single modality at a time and ignored sex-specific differences in aging patterns. In this work, we study human aging by leveraging comprehensive profiling of a unique and deeply phenotyped healthy human cohort of 10,000 individuals that includes clinical, physiological, behavioral, environmental, and multi-omic parameters. We devised machine learning models of chronological age and computed biological aging scores that represent diverse physiological systems and revealed different aging patterns among sexes. We identified significant differences in model performances between males and females and computed BA scores representing diverse physiological systems. Higher BA scores were associated with a higher prevalence of age-related medical conditions, highlighting the clinical relevance of these scores. Our analysis revealed system-specific aging dynamics and the potential of deeply phenotyped cohorts in accelerating our understanding of chronic diseases. Our findings present a more holistic view of the aging process, and lay the foundation for personalized medical prevention strategies.
